title: Vaping rates for schoolchildren appear to drop - is it falling out of favour?
content:
Vaping rates for schoolchildren appear to drop - is it falling out of favour?
- Published
For the first time in several years, the rates of vaping among schoolchildren in Wales appear to be falling.
The most recent data from a survey of more than 130,000 young people in secondary schools showed that across all age groups, habits are changing for both vaping and smoking.
Public health officials say the "significant fall" since 2023 coincides with the ban on disposable vapes being announced, though the impact of the law change is still being evaluated.
The findings are from the student health and well-being survey which has been carried out every two years by a research network made up of Public Health Wales, external, Cardiff University and the Welsh government.
Questions about vaping were added in 2017, and the survey carried out last year shows that 9,100 learners between Year 7 to 11 vape regularly, which is 3,200 fewer than 2023.
Meanwhile, the numbers smoking regularly have halved to 1,600.
The answers rely on self-reporting from young people, meaning the study depends on honesty and accurate recollection from participants, but it paints a snapshot of behaviours over nearly a decade.
Since the last survey in 2023, the proportion of learners in Years 7 to 11 who say they have tried a vape fell from 25.7% to 21%.
In the same period, the number who described themselves as regular vapers or smokers was much lower, and fell from 8% to 5.9%.
Officials said there has also been a faster drop in the numbers who said they smoke regularly, with the rate now just 1.8%.
So why are some young people turning away from vaping, after several years of the numbers going in the opposite direction?
Jay, 17, from Barry Sixth Form, in the Vale of Glamorgan, said he thinks his year group narrowly avoided the hype when vapes first became popular, but they are still far more popular among younger age groups.
"When we were in younger years (in school) it wasn't as common and so that's why I think a lot of people in our year feel like they don't need to do it," he said.
"Whereas I think younger people feel the peer pressure to do it, to fit in with their friend groups."
Amelie, also 17, said her peers in sixth form were more likely to be "more health conscious" which deters them from taking up vaping.
The figures also show higher rates of girls vaping than boys, despite the drop in numbers.
Amelie said colourful packaging was likely to play a part.
"I'd say it's because of the marketing and the product, colourful packages, flavours," she said.
"I'd say vaping is more targeted towards girls than boys."
But she added that lessons in school explaining the risks had been powerful.
She added: "Our school is very supportive, they've taken the correct steps to educate us, including the health education lessons, and they brought in a demonstration of what our lungs could look like - the 'popcorn' lung - so that helped."
Year 10 Whitmore High School student Harrison, 14, said he feels vaping has been normalised among younger people, and there can be pressure to vape.
As a keen footballer in Barry, the risks to his own health and his performance on the pitch have been big drivers for not vaping.
"Social media comes into it, a lot of people on Youtube and TikTok do it, they're smoking or vaping and people think that's cool to do," he said.
It's illegal for under-18s to buy the product, but he said access for some people wasn't difficult.
Anabella, 14, said she had definitely seen interest in vapes decline among her peers.
"I've seen a few people start to quit, people are starting to realise the health risks, and they're seeing the people they're around that do that sort of thing, aren't the people they should be around.
"Everyone was doing it so it was a trend, and now that it's died down, less people are starting in the first place."
Henriette Bertheux is responsible for personal and social education at Whitmore High, and said higher rates of boys being involved in extra-curricular sports was also likely to be a factor in fewer of them vaping, compared to girls.
At one point pupils were requesting frequent toilet trips as they would vape in pairs in the cubicles, which naturally also impacted their learning.
She said a combination of education around the health implications and tighter rules about how many children are allowed toilet breaks at once had helped reduce the problem.
"We had a year group that were targetted quite heavily when they were in year 7 and 8, it was coming on social media and they were susceptible to that," she said, adding that cohort had now left school
"We've definitely seen a drop in the younger years."
Mary-Ann McKibben from Public Health Wales said there had been a concerted effort from schools, public health agencies and government to curb vape use.
She said: "We've had the introduction of some quite strong legislation with the ban on disposable vapes last year and then a lot of publicity surrounding the Tobacco and Vapes Act, external that will be coming into place with restrictions on packaging, marketing and content and flavours of vapes going forward.
"That all influences behaviour change, together with a rising awareness of the harm that vapes can cause.
"Technically young people shouldn't be able to get hold of vapes through legitimate means if they're under 18, so often they are at risk of illicit products that are sold on the black market that may contain all sorts of contents that are even more toxic than the normal vapes.
"So be very, very careful in terms of what you're consuming because it could really damage your health."
She added it's also important that support is offered to young people who have been vaping nicotine products, because of their addictive qualities.

title: Incendios en Quito dejan 278 animales atendidos por la Unidad de Bienestar Animal
content:
Fecha de publicación:
Fecha de modificación:
La emergencia por los incendios forestales en Quito dejó 278 animales atendidos por equipos veterinarios de la Unidad de Bienestar Animal (UBA). Los profesionales realizaron controles de salud y atención veterinaria primaria en dos de las zonas afectadas por el fuego: el cerro Casitagua y La Vicentina.
Del total de animales atendidos, 265 recibieron atención en Casitagua y otros 13 en La Vicentina. Los equipos también recorrieron los sectores cercanos a los incendios para identificar animales que podían encontrarse en riesgo y orientaron a sus tutores sobre las medidas para mantenerlos seguros mientras duraba la emergencia.
En el cerro Casitagua, el incendio afectó aproximadamente 300 hectáreas. Los veterinarios de la UBA trabajaron durante todo el fin de semana y recorrieron los sectores afectados para localizar animales que pudieran necesitar atención o encontrarse en peligro.
Durante estas jornadas, los equipos encontraron a la mayoría de animales asustados y nerviosos por las llamas y el humo. Ante esta situación, los profesionales recomendaron a los tutores mantener a sus animales en lugares seguros. De preferencia, dentro de sus hogares.
La recomendación buscó reducir el riesgo de que los animales escaparan, se extraviaran o se desorientaran durante la emergencia. El humo y la presencia del fuego generaron condiciones que podían alterar su comportamiento, por lo que la UBA centró parte de su trabajo en verificar su estado y orientar a quienes estaban a su cargo.
Los equipos veterinarios también realizaron un rescate durante su intervención en Casitagua. Una hembra recién parida permanecía junto a sus nueve cachorros. El personal de la UBA trasladó a la madre y a sus crías a uno de los centros de la institución municipal.
En ese lugar, los animales reciben atención veterinaria y permanecen bajo cuidado. La intervención permitió que la hembra y sus nueve cachorros quedaran bajo supervisión del personal de la Unidad de Bienestar Animal.
La UBA también desplegó atención veterinaria en La Vicentina. En este sector, los equipos atendieron a 13 animales afectados principalmente por la presencia de humo.
Los profesionales realizaron evaluaciones físicas y controles para conocer el estado de salud de los animales. De esta manera, la atención se concentró en revisar posibles afectaciones relacionadas con las condiciones generadas por el incendio.
En ambos sectores, el trabajo de los equipos veterinarios incluyó la verificación de las condiciones de salud de los animales que permanecían en las zonas afectadas o en sus alrededores. Además, los profesionales entregaron recomendaciones a los tutores para protegerlos mientras continuaba la emergencia.
La Unidad de Bienestar Animal mantiene su articulación con las entidades municipales para responder ante situaciones de emergencia. Estas acciones buscan fortalecer la protección y el bienestar de los animales en el Distrito Metropolitano de Quito.

title: The human hands that keep this iconic clock ticking
content:
More than a timepiece, it has become a familiar witness to the city’s history, its chimes accompanying generations of Malaysians through moments both ordinary and momentous.
Today, the task of keeping it running falls to three men who continue the work of custodians before them.
Muhammad Kamarul Azman, L Kumarasamy and Roshdihisham Hassan, from the survey and mapping department, check, clean, wind and lubricate the century-old mechanism throughout the year.
“Every evening after office hours, we come here to wind the clock and make sure the time is accurate,” Kamarul told FMT.
Inside the narrow, sweltering tower, the trio take turns working the giant weights that keep the Gillett & Johnston clock ticking.
The task requires patience. According to Kamarul, the crank cannot be turned too quickly, as doing so could disrupt the pulley system. “That is why we rely on our own physical strength,” he said.
Their responsibility does not always end when the day’s checks are done. On one occasion, Kamarul had already returned home when a call came through informing him that the clock had stopped.
“I had already reached home when the building management called. So we had to come back at midnight to inspect it,” he recalled.
Their work takes on added meaning on the eve of Merdeka celebrations, when the clock becomes part of a national moment.
As crowds gather outside and the countdown begins, Kamarul, Kumarasamy and Roshdihisham stay inside the tower, watching closely to make sure the clock reaches midnight precisely as it should.
“At midnight, we really feel nervous. When we hear the people outside counting down, we feel proud from inside the tower,” Kamarul said.
It is a moment that turns an otherwise unseen job into something deeply personal: while thousands celebrate below, the men inside know the clock’s familiar chime depends, in part, on their hands.
Learning from those before them
For Kamarul, the role began almost by chance. When a senior colleague introduced him to the clock, seeing its century-old machinery at work sparked a fascination he had not expected.
“When you watch all the gears and machinery moving, you become very interested in learning how it all works. That is what has kept us here until today.”
There was no handbook to guide them; instead, much of what they know was learnt through experience and from those who cared for the clock before them.
And this knowledge matters because keeping the mechanism alive is not as simple as replacing a broken part.
“If any component is damaged, a replacement has to be specially made according to the original specifications because the parts are no longer available on the market,” Kamarul noted.
And so, year after year, the clock in this iconic building continues to tick – not only because of the machinery inside it, but because of the people who keep watch over it.

title: National Park Service director calls Yellowstone's wild bison recovery an 'incredible conservation story'
content:
A little more than a century ago, Yellowstone's bison were hanging on by a thread.
Today, thousands of them roam the park. And the conservation challenge has shifted from simply saving the herd to figuring out how to manage a thriving one.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS
During an interview with OutKick OutDoors, Jessica Bowron, acting director of the National Park Service, called the recovery an "incredible conservation story."
After millions of bison once roamed the Great Plains, the animals were nearly wiped out across their historic range. Rebuilding those populations, Bowron said, has taken decades of careful scientific work and cooperation among the Park Service and its Tribal, state, local and federal partners.
"To show up at Yellowstone today and have the experience as a visitor of seeing a wild bison in a functioning ecosystem, I don't know that we could have predicted that 100 years ago," Bowron said.
That's a pretty remarkable turnaround.
And now, Yellowstone's bison are helping build conservation herds far beyond the park itself.
Yellowstone bison are finding new homes
Through the Bison Conservation Transfer Program, Yellowstone works with Tribal partners to relocate live bison that have completed the necessary quarantine process.
Since 2019, more than 600 bison have been transferred to 29 tribes across 13 states, according to Bowron. More than 200 were transferred in 2026 alone.
"This is one of the coolest parts of this entire conservation effort," Bowron said.
Once the animals are transferred, she explained, each tribe can manage its herd according to its own priorities and sovereignty.
"It's a great example of how we're able to establish and expand conservation herds through that kind of partnership," Bowron said.
But conservation success doesn't mean the work is finished.
In some places, rebuilding the population remains the goal. At Yellowstone, Bowron said the challenge now is largely about managing the healthy herd that's already there.
"I think at Yellowstone, we're in the latter — figuring out how to successfully manage the herd that we have with all of our partners," she said.
At the same time, the Park Service continues to pursue live-transfer opportunities with tribes interested in establishing or expanding conservation herds.
A conservation problem you want to have
The Yellowstone story is also a reminder that conservation wins don't happen overnight.
Bowron said rebuilding bison populations has taken decades of scientific monitoring and cooperation among Tribal, state, local and federal partners.
WHY TED TURNER'S APPROACH TO CONSERVATION IS THE MINDSET AMERICA DESPERATELY NEEDS RIGHT NOW
And even after a species rebounds, the work changes rather than disappears.
For generations, the question was whether wild bison could survive at all in places like Yellowstone.
Now, wildlife managers are dealing with a very different question: What do you do when the comeback works?
Bison don't care where Yellowstone's boundary lines are drawn. They move across a massive landscape, meaning managing a successful herd requires cooperation among the Park Service and the many communities and agencies surrounding it.
But the fact that there is a healthy herd to manage — and enough animals to help establish conservation herds elsewhere — would have been difficult to imagine a century ago.
For anyone who's ever sat in Yellowstone traffic because a bison decided the middle of the road belonged to him, it might be easy to forget just how close America came to losing that experience entirely.

Today, seeing those animals wander through the park feels almost inevitable.
It wasn't always.
So yeah, you can definitely call it a comeback.

title: If India Is Spending Crores on Its Cities, Nature Must Count as Infrastructure
content:
Indian cities have a familiar response to flooding, heat and water stress—build more. Bigger drains, higher embankments, longer pipelines and more concrete infrastructure are often treated as the default answer.
But India is now at a moment when that instinct must be reconsidered.
The Union government’s Rs 1 lakh crore Urban Challenge Fund, operationalised in April 2026, is intended to catalyse about Rs 4 lakh crore of urban investment over five years.
Central assistance can cover 25 percent of project cost, while at least 50 percent is expected from market sources. Its ambition is to create resilient, productive, inclusive and climate-responsive cities.
That is a major opportunity. It also raises a basic question: when cities compete for finance, what will count as infrastructure?
A flyover has a project cost. A sewage plant has a contract. A restored wetland, urban lake, floodplain or green corridor may reduce flooding, cool neighbourhoods and recharge groundwater, but those benefits are harder to place on a municipal balance sheet.
If “bankability” is interpreted too narrowly, India could end up financing what is easiest to monetise rather than what makes cities most resilient.
Nature Already Performs Urban Services
The case is especially clear in urban flooding. In July, the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs acknowledged that intense rainfall is only part of the problem. Unplanned growth, encroachment of natural water bodies and inadequate drainage also compound flooding. The ministry’s own river-centric planning guidance recognises nature-based solutions.
Yet wetlands, lakes, floodplains and permeable open spaces are still too often treated as environmental amenities rather than working urban assets.
A wetland can temporarily store stormwater. A floodplain gives a river room to expand. Vegetated areas slow runoff and help water infiltrate the soil. Trees and green spaces can reduce local heat exposure. These services do not eliminate the need for drains, pumps or engineered flood protection. But they can reduce the burden placed on them.
The choice, therefore, is not nature versus engineering. The smarter model is blue-green-grey infrastructure, where ecological and engineered systems are planned together.
This matters because India’s new urban finance architecture is explicitly market-linked. Nature-based projects often struggle not because they lack public value, but because avoided flood losses, lower heat exposure and groundwater recharge do not produce simple cash flows.
A 2026 guidebook from the India Forum for Nature-based Solutions also highlighted the need to strengthen financing models if urban NbS are to scale.
Make Nature Investible, Without Turning it into a Slogan
The Urban Challenge Fund can help change this, but only if natural infrastructure is deliberately built into project appraisal.
- First, eligible projects should be able to include restoration of wetlands, lakes, river buffers, watersheds and urban green systems as core infrastructure components, not decorative add-ons.
- Second, appraisal should recognise avoided costs and public benefits.
If restoring a wetland reduces peak runoff and lowers the need for additional drainage, that value should be visible in the economic assessment.
- Third, cities seeking finance for major flood-management or heat-resilience projects should show that nature-based and hybrid alternatives were assessed alongside conventional engineering options.
This does not mean forcing a green solution where it will not work. It means asking the question before automatically reaching for concrete.
- Fourth, nature-based projects must be measured as rigorously as conventional infrastructure.
Funding should be tied to outcomes such as water retained, flood exposure reduced, canopy maintained, or temperature moderated. Planting trees or fencing a lake cannot, by itself, be treated as success.
Calling something “nature-based” does not make it effective. Poorly designed restoration can fail just as poorly designed grey infrastructure can.
The Money Is Arriving. The Rules Should Reward Resilience
The Urban Challenge Fund matters not only because of its size, but because it can influence what municipalities and investors begin to consider financeable.
If urban resilience is judged mainly through assets that generate direct revenue, natural systems will remain underfunded even when they provide essential public services. But if city finance begins recognising reduced risk, avoided costs and measurable resilience outcomes, wetlands, floodplains and urban forests can move from the margins of environmental planning into the centre of infrastructure strategy.
India does not need to choose between concrete and nature. It needs to stop financing cities as though only one of them counts.
If Rs 1 lakh crore of public support is going to reshape urban India, it should help build cities that work with their natural systems, not cities that pay to replace them after they are gone.
(The author is a Senior Associate Fellow, Land Resources Division, The Energy and Resources Institute (TERI). This is an opinion piece, and the views expressed above are the author’s own. The Quint neither endorses nor is responsible for the same.)

title: „Þetta er lögbundin þjónusta sem við eigum áfram að veita – án fjármagns?“
content: Samkvæmt nýja fjárlagafrumvarpinu missa sveitarfélögin 1,1 milljarð króna á ári frá ríkissjóði sem áður var eyrnamerktur verkefnum sveitarfélaga við farsæld barna sem þurfa sértækan samhæfðan stuðning. Verkefnastjóri farsældar segir niðurskurðinn setja fjölskyldur og börn sem þurfi á stuðningi að halda í afleita biðstöðu.Á við um 6000 börn á landinu öllu og fjölskyldur þeirraÍ farsældarlögum sem tóku gildi árið 2021 var kveðið á um styrk til sveitarfélaga frá ríkinu. Styrkurinn fór í að innleiða farsældarlögin og ráða starfsfólk eins og málstjóra sem halda utan um alla þræði sem snúa að börnum sem þurfa á stuðningi að halda og fjölskyldum þeirra. Markmiðið er að þau fái samþætta og viðeigandi þjónustu á réttum tíma, þannig að þau falli ekki á milli kerfa og létta álagi af foreldrum svo þeir geti sinnt sinni vinnu. Stuðningurinn á við um 6000 börn á landinu öllu. Þetta eru langveik börn, börn með fötlun eða aðrar takmarkanir, erfiðar heimilisaðstæður og fleira.Rúmlega milljarður sem sveitarfélög gerðu ráð fyrir frá ríkinu í farsæld barna með stuðningsþarfir er skorinn niður í fjárlagafrumvarpi næsta árs. Ráðherra segir fé veitt eftir öðrum leiðum.„Enginn sem bjóst við að þessir útreikningar myndu fara niður í 0 kr.“Sólveig Norðfjörð starfar sem verkefnastjóri farsældar fyrir nokkur sveitarfélög. Henni brá þegar hún sá að ekki er gert ráð fyrir styrknum í nýju fjárlagafrumvarpi.„Já, okkur brá. Eftir að innleiðingunni lýkur þá var alltaf gert ráð fyrir því að við myndum fá framlög frá ríkinu. Í lögum um jöfnunarsjóð kemur fram að umframkostnaður vegna samþættingar þjónustu eigi að koma þangað til að við erum farin að sjá fjárhagslegan ávinning af verkefninu. Við vissum að það yrði einhver endurútreikningur en það var enginn sem bjóst við að þessir útreikningar myndu fara niður í 0 kr. fyrir öll sveitarfélögin,“ segir Sólveig.Sjá fram á uppsagnir og skerta þjónustu við börnHún bendir á að í skýrslu Ríkisendurskoðunar frá júní 2026 komi fram að ríkið þurfi áfram að styðja sveitarfélögin við innleiðingu farsældarlaganna.„Við erum bara að reyna að finna út úr því hvað við getum gert og vonum auðvitað að þetta endi ekki svona. En ég reikna með að það hljóti að þurfa að segja upp fólki. Það er búið að ráða fólk inn í skólana svo að þetta hefur mikil áhrif og mun skerða þjónustu við börn og fjölskyldur þeirra,“ segir Sólveig.Enn sé verið að vinna með mjög þung mál inni í Barnavernd og í skólunum og allt sé gert til að samþætta þá sértæku stuðningsþjónustu sem börnin og fjölskyldur þeirra þurfa. Þetta sé allt gert til að reyna að koma í veg fyrir alvarleg áhrif sem geta komið fram síðar með tilheyrandi þungum kostnaði fyrir ríkissjóð. Kosnaði sem rennur til að mynda í örorku foreldra og dýrum úrræðum fyrir börn sem gætu verið óþörf ef vel er að farsældinni staðið.„Þetta er lögbundin þjónusta sem við eigum áfram að veita – án fjármagns. Við sjáum ekki fram á að geta veitt sömu þjónustuna án áframhaldandi stuðnings í þessu verkefni frá ríkissjóði til sveitarfélaganna,“ segir Sólveig.Miklu fjármagni veitt eftir öðrum leiðumInga Sæland, barnamálaráðherra segir að þrátt fyrir að framlag í jöfnunarsjóðinn (1,1 milljarður króna) hafi verið fellt brott sé verið að setja umtalsvert meira fjármagn í aukna þjónustu og farsæld barna með öðrum leiðum.Hverju svarar þú þessum félagsfræðingum, skólastjórnendum og verkefnastjórum farsældar í sveitarfélögunum sem segja að þarna sé verið að þurrka út fjármagn sem þau gerðu ráð fyrir að kæmi frá ríkinu til sveitarfélaganna til að halda áfram því starfi sem þau hafa komið á koppinn en er hvergi nærri lokið?„Það er meira en komið á koppinn það gengur mjög vel víða. Það eru yfir 6000 börn sem þegar eru farin að nýta sér þessa þjónustu, þessa snemmtæku íhlutun sem er orðin að veruleika. Ég segi að sveitarfélögin eru algjörlega komin á þann stað að geta tekið utan um þetta sjálf og ég hvet þessa aðila til að skoða allt þetta fjármagn sem við raunverulega erum að setja inn í sveitarfélögin okkar,“ segir Inga Sæland.Innleiðingartímabilinu ljúki um áramótBarnamálaráðherra áréttar að um áramót sé innleiðingartímabili farsældarlaganna lokið. Fjármagn verði nú veitt til sveitarfélaganna með öðrum hætti.Þá hafi verið lögð fram á Alþingi framkvæmdaáætlun um farsæld bara til ársins 2030 með 16 aðgerðum sem séu að fullu fjármagnaðar.700 milljónir króna fari enn í verkefni tengd farsæld barna, en renna ekki beint til sveitarfélaganna.Til standi að styrkja þjónustu við börn með fjölþættan vanda um 800 milljónir króna til viðbótar við þá 3,7 milljarða sem þegar hefur verið samið um.Barna- og fjölskyldustofa fái 1 milljarð króna aukalega í fjárlögum næsta árs.400 milljónum króna verði bætt í þjónustu við börn í viðkvæmri stöðu.350 milljónir verða settar í að stytta biðtíma eftir þjónustu við börn.Og svo vill barnamálaráðherra auglýsa 500 milljónir króna sem sveitarfélögin geta sótt um til að styðja við farsæld barna og aðgerðir gegn ofbeldi.Ráðherra telur að sveitarfélögin muni hagræða og forgangsraða í þágu farsældar barna„Þetta eru miklir fjármunir sem við erum að setja í málaflokkinn, mjög miklir þannig að þegar við erum að tala um stuðning við ákveðið innleiðingarferli sem þegar hefur verið í 5 ár og er talið að eigi að ljúka um áramótin þá teljum við ekki ástæðu til að halda því í því formi áfram heldur erum við að koma með fjármuni í öðru formi,“ segir Inga.En sveitarstjórnarfólk sem við höfum rætt við og þessir félagsfræðingar hafa bent á að sveitarfélögin eru búin að leggja út í mikinn kostnað og hafa ráðið til sín fólk, þessa málstjóra og starfsfólk sem á að sinna þessu og hafa núna áhyggjur af því að geta ekki fjármagnað launakostnað og annað sem að þessu snýr út af þessari breytingu í fjárlagafrumvarpinu?„Já, ég tel að þau muni alveg standa sig í því og hafi borð fyrir báru og þau eru ekki síður klók eins og við hin í að hagræða og forgangsraða fjármununum sínum og ég treysti þeim alveg til þess að ráða fram úr þessu,“ svarar Inga.En hvaða áhrif mun þetta hafa á börn og fjölskyldur sem þurfa á þessu að halda? Mun vera samfella í þeirra þjónustu áfram þrátt fyrir þetta?Já, ég hef 100% trú á því. Algjör samfella og ekkert þjónusturof heldur snemmtæk íhlutun áfram. Þannig að ég hef engar áhyggjur af því að við eigum ekki eftir að standa okkur saman, segir Inga.

title: Fruitcorso Tiel wordt fruitfestival: stilstaande kunstwerken om kosten te drukken
content: Voor Tielenaren met een hang naar traditie moet het even wennen zijn: dit jaar reden er geen praalwagens vol fruit door Tiel voor het jaarlijkse fruitcorso. De kunstwerken van fruit staan voor het eerst stil. Bezoekers mogen er zelf langs wandelen om ze te bekijken. Het jaarlijkse fruitcorso in de Gelderse plaats heeft na zo'n 70 jaar plaats gemaakt voor een fruitfestival. "Dat we geen rijdend corso hebben, missen de Tielenaren heel erg", zegt een bezoekster van het festival. "Rijdend is toch mooier dan stilstaand", zegt een ander. Op de kaart Die reacties zijn niet gek. Het fruitcorso reed immers al sinds 1961 in september door Tiel. Het corso diende in de beginjaren als een lokale oogstviering. De praalwagens die waren versierd met groente en fruit uit de regio dienden een doel: Tiel op de kaart zetten. Maar deze opzet werd te duur en te ingewikkeld, voornamelijk door sterk gestegen kosten voor veiligheid. De organisatie zou hekken moeten plaatsen en verkeersregelaars inzetten. Ook waren er niet genoeg vrijwilligers te vinden. Uiteindelijk betekent niet rijden maar stilstaan een kostenbesparing van 200.000 euro. "De kosten liepen heel snel op, waardoor het uiteindelijk niet meer financieel verantwoord was", zegt bestuurslid Dennis Voorendt. Toch is hij tevreden met de nieuwe opzet. "We hebben gisteren een hele drukbezochte dag gehad. Vanaf het begin is het hier gewoon een gezellige drukte geweest." Meer theater Gisteravond was ook de zogenoemde By Night-versie van het festival. "Dat is weer een hele andere beleving met allemaal lichtjes", zegt Voorendt. "Dat geeft het iets heel feeërieks." Beelden van gisteravond: Ook zijn er nog andere voordelen, ziet corsobouwer Jochem Schoots. "Nu kun je echt een voorstelling laten zien bij een fruitkunstwerk, veel meer theater. Je kunt mensen meenemen in het verhaal." Morgen is de laatste dag van het festival in de nieuwe opzet.
